nameStory: The name 'cusk' comes from an old Scottish word for this deep-water cod relative. It's also called 'tusk' in some places, referring to its prominent canine-like teeth that give it a somewhat fierce appearance.
description: The cusk is a deep-water cod relative that looks like a cross between a cod and an eel. It has an elongated, somewhat compressed body that can reach up to 3 feet long, with a continuous fin running along its back and around its tail. Its most distinctive feature is a single long barbel hanging from its chin, like a whisker, and it typically displays a mottled brown to yellowish coloration.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated and somewhat eel-like but deeper than a true eel, with a compressed body that feels firm and muscular to the touch

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single continuous dorsal fin runs along the entire back and connects around the tail - no gaps or separate fin sections like most cod family members

idTips.label: Barbel
idTips.description: One prominent barbel (whisker-like projection) hangs from the center of the chin, feeling fleshy and flexible when touched

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Mottled brown, yellowish-brown, or sometimes reddish-brown with darker irregular blotches and a lighter belly

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Terminal mouth with prominent canine-like teeth that feel sharp to the touch - larger than typical cod teeth

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 1-3 feet long when caught, with a solid, weighty feel for its length due to its deep body

habitat: Cusk live in deep, cold waters along the continental shelf and slope, typically found at depths of 300-1000 feet off New England's coast. They prefer rocky bottoms and are usually caught by deep-sea fishermen rather than shore anglers. In New England waters, they're most commonly encountered from the Gulf of Maine northward.

seasonality.spring: May move to slightly shallower waters for spawning. Most active feeding period begins as water temperatures stabilize.
seasonality.summer: Peak fishing season when they're most accessible to recreational deep-sea fishing boats in their typical depth range.
seasonality.fall: Continue to feed actively in preparation for winter. Still commonly caught by deep-water fishing operations.
seasonality.winter: Retreat to deepest parts of their range. Less commonly encountered except by commercial fishing vessels.

funFact: Cusk are the only fish in their genus worldwide - they're so unique that scientists gave them their own private category with no close relatives sharing their exact body plan and fin arrangement.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small cod or haddock, but the continuous fin running around the tail is the dead giveaway - cod family members have separate, distinct fins. Remember: 'Cusk = continuous, cod = cut up into separate fins.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'tusk' in some regions, cusk are completely unrelated to the Arctic marine mammal called walrus (whose tusks are actually enlarged teeth). The fish's 'tusk' nickname refers only to its prominent canine teeth.
compareHints: As the only member of genus Brosme, cusk are unique among New England fish. Compared to their closest relatives in the hake and burbot family, cusk have the distinctive continuous fin arrangement and are strictly marine, while burbot (their closest relative) live in freshwater and have two separate dorsal fins.
